summary.text: Protein folding is how a chain of amino acids, once a ribosome has made it, changes from an unstable random coil into an ordered three-dimensional structure.
The amino acid sequence determines the final native structure, and the correct structure is essential for the protein to work.
When folding fails the protein is generally inactive, and accumulated fibrils of misfolded proteins are believed to cause several neurodegenerative diseases.

facts.value: Secondary structure forms first, as helices and sheets

items.prompt: Where does the information for how a protein folds come from?

options.label: The ribosome that happened to make it
The temperature of the room alone
The order of its own amino acids
The cell wall around the cell

items.explain: The amino acid sequence of each protein contains the information that specifies both the native structure and the pathway to reach it.

items.prompt: Cooking an egg changes the proteins inside it. What best describes the change?

options.label: They shift from a folded state to an unfolded one
They fold into a tighter, more ordered shape
They are built into longer polypeptide chains
They are freshly made by ribosomes

items.explain: Denaturation is a transition from a folded to an unfolded state, and it happens in cooking.

items.prompt: A protein fails to fold into its native structure. What is the usual result?

options.label: It always becomes toxic
It refolds on its own at once
It becomes a stronger enzyme
It generally ends up inactive

items.explain: Failure to fold into a native structure generally produces inactive proteins, though a few misfolded ones gain a modified or toxic function.

items.prompt: Helices and sheets have a water-loving side and a water-fearing side. When a protein folds, where do the water-fearing sides go?

options.label: Out toward the surrounding water
Packed together in the protein's inner core
Spread evenly over the whole surface
Out past the end of the chain

items.explain: Folding places the hydrophilic sides facing the surrounding water and the hydrophobic sides facing the hydrophobic core.

items.prompt: A ribosome is still building the far end of a chain. Can the front part already be folding?

options.label: Yes, folding often starts while the rest is still being made
No, folding only starts after a finished chain is released
No, folding needs chaperones before it can start
Yes, but only once the far end has been completed

items.explain: Folding of many proteins begins during translation, so the front folds while the far end is still being synthesized.

paragraphs.heading: What folding is
paragraphs.text: A ribosome builds a protein as a straight chain of amino acids. Protein folding is the physical process in which that chain goes from an unstable random coil to an ordered three-dimensional shape. That shape is what lets the protein do its job. For many proteins, folding starts while the chain is still being made. The finished, well-defined shape is called the protein's native state.

paragraphs.heading: The sequence holds the plan
paragraphs.text: A protein's primary structure, its order of amino acids, decides its native shape. Which amino acids appear, and where they sit along the chain, settles which parts fold up close together. The order matters more than the overall mix of amino acids. In the end, the sequence carries the information for both the final shape and the route to reach it. Surroundings count too, though: similar proteins can fold differently depending on where they are.

paragraphs.heading: Helices and sheets
paragraphs.text: The first step toward the native shape is forming secondary structure. Its typical forms are alpha helices and beta sheets, which fold quickly because hydrogen bonds inside the molecule hold them steady, as Linus Pauling first described. In a helix, the backbone forms hydrogen bonds that twist it into a spiral. In a beta sheet, the backbone bends back over itself to make those bonds. The bonds link the amide hydrogen and the carbonyl oxygen of the peptide bond.

paragraphs.heading: Packing into a final shape
paragraphs.text: Helices and sheets are often amphipathic: one side is drawn to water and the other side avoids it. That helps build tertiary structure, in which the chain folds so the water-loving sides face the watery surroundings and the water-avoiding sides face the protein's core. Once that shape is set, two cysteine residues may also be tied together by a covalent disulfide bridge. In some proteins, several folded chains then come together to form quaternary structure and a fully working protein.

paragraphs.heading: What drives it
paragraphs.text: Folding happens on its own. It is guided mainly by hydrophobic interactions, hydrogen bonds within the molecule and van der Waals forces, while conformational entropy works against it. Because it is spontaneous, folding must have a negative Gibbs free energy. It also depends on the setting: the solvent, the salt level, the pH, the temperature, and whether cofactors and molecular chaperones are present.

paragraphs.heading: Fast and slow
paragraphs.text: How long folding takes varies enormously from one protein to another. Studied outside the cell, the slowest proteins need many minutes or hours, mostly because of proline isomerization, and pass through several in-between states on the way. Very small proteins of up to a hundred amino acids with a single domain usually fold in one step. Milliseconds are the norm, and the fastest known folding finishes within a few microseconds.

paragraphs.heading: When folding fails
paragraphs.text: A protein that fails to reach its native shape is usually inactive, but sometimes a misfolded protein gains a changed or toxic function. Several neurodegenerative and other diseases are thought to come from a buildup of amyloid fibrils made of misfolded proteins; the infectious kinds are called prions. Folding can also run in reverse. Denaturation, the change from folded to unfolded, happens in cooking and in burns.
